title: Egg omelet with cheese and meat, cooked in animal fat

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet with cheese and meat, cooked in animal fat, is a dish where eggs are beaten with cheese and diced meat, then fried in rendered animal fat or meat drippings. This method gives the omelet a rich flavor and aroma typical of traditional meals popular in the late 1990s.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was a common quick breakfast in cafeterias and diners during the 1990s.
Animal fat used for frying increases caloric density and enhances taste compared with vegetable oils.
Cream cheese was usually added in modest amounts so as not to overpower the meat flavor.
Typical meats included ham, bacon, or sausage pieces.
Omelets were often served with potatoes, bread, or vegetables as a side.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: The dish contains vitamins B2, B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Meat and eggs are good sources of iron and zinc, important for immunity and blood formation.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese adds calcium, contributing to bone and teeth health.

items.title: Energy-dense
items.content: Animal fat raises the calorie content, which can be beneficial for those with high energy needs.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Frying in animal fat increases saturated fat intake, which may affect cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Caloric load
items.content: The dish is very calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs or dairy proteins may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using cured meats can add significant salt, which is a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, cut into portions. It pairs well with toast, boiled potatoes, fresh vegetables, or herbs. Optional condiments include ketchup, mustard, or a light hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat gently with a little added fat to restore flavor.
